newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Labor reveals budget vote plans.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Labor reveals budget vote plans.

text.p: The Australian Labor opposition on Friday revealed the fiscal cuts it would try to vote down when the government's deficit-slashing budget appears in the Senate, the upper house of parliament.
Opposition Leader Kim Beazley told reporters there were other measures which Labor disliked, but which were invulnerable to Senate obstruction for constitutional reasons.
"We fully acknowledge, understand but not approve the fact that the vast bulk of the cuts to public programmes put in place by this government will go through," Beazley said.
"That's because they're locked up in appropriation bills or legislation that one way or another is not possible to oppose reasonably. You'd create a national crisis if you attempted to do so."
The Liberal-National government's August 20 budget implemented measures that would save A$3.9 billion in the fiscal year to June 1997 and A$7.2 billion in 1997/98.
By 1998/99 the fiscal programme is supposed to produce a A$1 billion underlying surplus -- that is, without asset sales.
Parliament resumes sitting on Monday to consider the budget.
Beazley told reporters that Labor would oppose these measures (which are shown with their value to the budget for 1997/98, their first full year of implementation):
-- Reduced tax incentives for research and development; A$430 million;
-- Faster repayment of student's loans, A$230 million;
-- Reduced childcare assistance, A$147 million;
-- A requirement for residents to contribute to nursing home costs, A$125 million.
-- Income from retirement savings to be counted in assessing pension entitlements, A$93 million;

Opposition treasury spokesman Gareth Evans told reporters the measures that Labor opposed were worth about A$7.3 billion over the four years from June 1996, compared with an estimated A$23.4 billion for all of the government's budget measures.
Labor cannot alone obstruct the budget bills; it needs the support of all but two of the other non-government senators to do so.
The other players in the Senate are the seven left-leaning Australian Democrats, two loosely united Greens and a pair of Independents.
-- Higher charges for university students, A$66 million;
-- Tightened elibigility for student income support, A$60 million;
-- Increased patient payments for medicines under national health insurance, A$52 million;
-- A cancelled bounty for the computer industry, A$20 million;
-- A cancelled bounty on shipbuilding, A$6 million.
New revenue measures are susceptible to Senate obstruction because they always require legislation.
Similarly, spending changes can be blocked if legislation is required to change some kind of entitlement, such as social security eligibility rules.

But expenditure cuts cannot be blocked if they appear only in the usual appropriations (or supply) bills by which parliament regularly authorises government spending. Obstruction of such bills would spark a constitutional crisis.
Even if the bills were changed to authorise more spending, there is no way the Senate could force the government to spend the money.
"There are many more measures that we would like to knock off on the outlay side but which are inaccessible to that kind of attack," Evans said.
Evans has previously said that the overall shape of the budget would survive the Senate, although measures worth a few hundred million Australian dollars might be lost.
